utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. On Wednesday, I would like to welcome everybody, the accused, the counsel, members of the OTP, anybody who is assisting us. I would like to give the floor to Ms. Tomic, the Defence counsel for Mr. Coric. She's going to continue presenting her final arguments. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and around the courtroom who are observing these proceedings. At the beginning of today's argument, I would like to correct two numbers that I read out incorrectly. I would like to do it for the transcript. The mistake is on transcript page 52, lines 5 and 6. In connection with Witness Skender, the following transcript pages should be referred to: 45210 through 45283, and not 45310 and 45283. Likewise, on transcript page 76, line 4, instead of P2574, there should be P2754. Your Honours, the Prosecutor, in their final brief, paragraph 1041, as well as in their closing argument, assert that the HVO tolerated crimes because it was the HVO policy. It tolerated war crimes and crimes against humanity, and thus it did not instigate proceedings for such crimes. Instead, and only rarely, it prosecuted perpetrators of minor offences. The Prosecutor furthermore alleges that the accused Valentin Coric is directly responsible for such doings and that in that way, he directly contributed to the joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecutor asserts that there was an obligation for proceedings to be instigated against perpetrators of such crimes and that that was regulated by the International Humanitarian Law. The fact that proceedings were instigated for crimes regulated by domestic laws does not diminish the responsibility of the accused. In order to support their thesis, the Prosecutor invoked the first-instance judgement in the Milutinovic case. It should be pointed out that that judgement is a first-instance judgement and that the appeals judgement is still pending. Furthermore, the Milutinovic case arose from Serbia and Yugoslavia, and the Penal Code of those states is different from the Penal Code that was in effect in the area and at the time relevant for the Prlic et al case. The Coric Defence would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to a more relevant legal authority, and those are the final conclusions from the first-instance decision in the Hadzihasanovic/Kubura case, because that judgement and those conclusions are relative to the same space and the same time as our case. In paragraph 261 of that judgement, it says: "Consequently, at the time the acts alleged in the indictment were committed, there was no binding obligation on states and, therefore, on the Courts in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to prosecute individuals for war crimes under customary International Law." Your Honours, it stems from this that national judiciary bodies had the right and had the authority to decide whether crimes should be qualified as war crimes or, alternatively, they would be qualified as regular crimes, so to speak. In other words, the Prosecutor is not right when he claims that the fact that crime reports were filed for regular crimes, and not for war crimes, leads to one and only conclusion, and that is that there was a criminal intent beyond any reasonable doubt and, hence, that there was also criminal responsibility. In any case, the Prosecutor didn't do anything to investigate or lead evidence about the types of criminal reports filed. That did not prevent him from misinterpreting the facts and saying that such criminal reports did not even exist. Your Honours, a more detailed analysis of a limited number of pieces of evidence that the Defence has managed to obtain demonstrates that such reports were indeed filed by appropriate bodies pursuant to the Penal Code of the SFRY. The Coric Defence tendered into evidence log-books and registers of some prosecutor offices. They are on the file as Exhibit 5D4288. Due to its limited resources, the Defence was not in a position to obtain the registries of all courts and all prosecutors' offices. If we had been able to do so, that would certainly help the Trial Chamber to create an integral picture of what really went on. These registers, in the part that concerns proceedings against unknown perpetrators, there is a reference to four proceedings that were instigated for crimes pursuant to Article 142 of the Penal Code of the SFRY. These cases may be located under the following numbers: KTN-3/95, KTN-99/95, KTN-101/95, and KTN-103/95. In all of the cases, the criminal reports were filed in 1993, which is also visible in the register. It has also been noted that one case, under number KTN-98/95, was instigated for a crime pursuant to Article 144 of the same law. In all the five cases, the agreed parties or victims were Muslims. Article 142 of the Penal Code of the SFRY concerns the crime known as a war crime against civilian population. Article 144 of the same Code concerns a crime of war crime against prisoners of war. Your Honours, this clearly shows that the Prosecutor is wrong when he claims that no single proceedings were instigated for war crimes. With regard to the quantity of the pieces of evidence that the Coric Defence has managed to obtain and tender into evidence, I would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to another paragraph from the aforementioned judgement in the Hadzihasanovic/Kubura case, paragraph 239. In that sense, Hadzihasanovic's Defence, in its own interests, has to answer charges against the accused Hadzihasanovic, and it can present documents that testify to the measures that the accused Hadzihasanovic undertook in order to, for example, elucidate the context of the case or the fact that the military disciplinary system was in place, it was up and running. However, the fact that the Defence presented such documents should certainly not be at its detriment. There is one thing to take into account the necessity for the accused to answer the charges against him. However, burden of proof cannot be transferred onto the Hadzihasanovic Defence and thus put it in a hopeless situation. On the one hand, if the Defence presents a certain number of documents which show that measures were indeed taken, the Prosecutor will reap benefits from the lack of evidence in its case. On the other hand, if the Hadzihasanovic Defence opts for a passive defence and it doesn't present documents that demonstrate that measures were indeed taken, the Prosecutor can use such a situation in order to establish that the accused Hadzihasanovic did not take any measures at all, since his own Defence failed to locate a single document that might have proven that he had. The Prosecutor, as I've already stated, by its allegations, implies that Valentin Coric was responsible for the fact that perpetrators of various crimes were not prosecuted and punished, and I'm going to quote another part of the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura judgement. Paragraph 137: "To determine measures a superior must take, an examination of national law is relevant." 139, paragraph 139: "Besides, in order to determine the scope of the measures a superior could take to determine his own responsibility under Article 7(3), the Tribunal's case law has relied on the national law and/or regulations of one of the armed forces in conflict." At the time relevant for the indictment, across the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the HZ-HB, the area was regulated by the same laws and regulations; the Law on Criminal Proceedings, the Penal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Penal Code of the SFRY. This is corroborated by documents P449, P592, 2D908, 2D909 and 2D910. The Law on Criminal Proceedings, which is also Exhibit 4D1105, regulated the rights and obligations of authorised bodies in the following way: In keeping with Articles 158 and 161, investigations were instigated at the request of the prosecutor, and the person in charge of investigations was the investigating judge. An investigating judge was duty-bound to inform the prosecutor if, during the investigation, it was established that the proceedings had to be expanded to include another crime or other persons. This is regulated by Article 165 of the same law. According to Article 170, an investigating judge could stop an investigation at the request of a prosecutor. In special cases regulated by Article 171, that could be done by a trial chamber. Once an investigation was completed, the investigating judge in charge would refer the case to the prosecutor, and that was regulated by Article 174. Article 261 stipulated that the proceedings before a court were conducted based on an indictment issued by the public prosecutor or by the victim of the crime. The prosecutor was the one who qualified a crime, who gave it a legal name, referring to a provision in the Penal Code, which also meant that those provisions had to be applied upon the prosecutor's proposal. That was prescribed by Article 262. A judgement was handed down by the court. When handing down a judgement, the court did not have to abide by the prosecutor's proposals about the legal qualification of the crime. This is regulated in Article 346. Your Honours, it arises from all of that that Valentin Coric, the Military Police Administration, or any member of the military police did not have the authority to issue indictments, to conduct investigations, or to stop criminal proceedings. They also did not have the authority to qualify crimes or issue judgements. This means that Valentin Coric, the Military Police Administration and military policemen did not have a say in deciding what kind of proceedings would be conducted. They didn't decide about who will be punished, whether they will be punished, and how they will be punished. It was the judiciary that had all those authorities, both the military and civilian prosecutors as well as judges, including investigating judges. None of the aforementioned judiciary bodies were part of the structures of the Military Police Administration or the military police units. Valentin Coric did not have any authority over those judiciary bodies. He was also not in a position to control them, either de jure or de facto. The military police was just one of the bodies who could file a criminal report with a competent prosecutor's office after the end of a police investigation, and that is where all the obligations, authorities and possibilities given to the military police to contribute to the prosecution of criminals stopped. Under the same factual circumstances, by studying and reviewing the same regulations, the Trial Chamber in the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case, in paragraph 1061, concluded as follows: "The Chamber finds that the accused Hadzihasanovic was unable to carry out his own criminal investigation or to influence how the case was dealt with by Judge Mirsad Strika or the competent prosecutor. Given that the 3rd Corps military police informed the investigating judge of the arrival of the bodies at the Zenica Morgue, thereby referring the matter to the appropriate military judicial authority, it cannot be concluded that the accused Hadzihasanovic did not take the necessary and reasonable measures under Article 7(3) of the Statute." Your Honours, in this case there is evidence that numerous criminal reports were submitted against perpetrators of crimes, including those crimes where the victims were Muslims. By far, the largest percentage of those were initiated by the military police by submitting those very criminal reports. Tomljanovich, who was a Prosecution expert, at pages 6368 and 6369 of the transcript, as well as the OTP Witness Biskic at transcript pages 15277 and 15278, confirmed that the military police submitted over 1.000 criminal reports in 1992 alone. It is also confirmed by document P950. The Defence Witness NO, in his testimony at page 51215 and 51216 of the transcript, stated that according to his knowledge, the military police submitted over 2.000 criminal reports. Valentin Coric's Defence would like to remind the Trial Chamber that during our examination of Witness Vidovic at transcript pages 51438 to 51535, and its examination of Witness Buntic at transcript pages 30516 to 30568, presented those witnesses a number of documents which had to do with around 40 criminal proceedings held against various perpetrators for crimes the victims of which were Muslims; inter alia, it included the crimes of murder, rape, theft, et cetera. Due to limited time, this Defence is not in a position to present all those documents yet again to the Trial Chamber. Besides, in Exhibit 5D4288, that is to say, in the KTN prosecution registers, one can see that during the period of time relevant to this indictment, 296 criminal reports were submitted in total for various crimes committed against Muslims. Most of them were submitted by the military police. Your Honours, in their closing arguments at page 52132 of the transcript, the Prosecution stated that they agree that in the Military Police Administration, the various companies, and the 5th Military Police Battalion, there were good men who were trying to perform their jobs well. The Prosecution also stated that they were trying to do something against this widespread criminal behaviour in the field. The Prosecution also said that it was for that reason that they drafted all the reports we watched, we saw. Your Honours, the Coric Defence asserts that evidence shows that the position to prosecute perpetrators of crimes, and a general condemnation of unlawful conduct, was the only plan Valentin Coric had as well as the only plan that existed within the Military Police Administration and the military police of the HVO as a whole. It was not a position of a few good men. I'd like to remind you of the words of Witness Andabak at transcript pages 50953 to 50954: [In English] "Yes, I do know about that, and it was the position of the military police, from the top man, Mr. Coric, was that any such perpetrators should be persecuted and the criminal report filed, and for them to be dismissed from the unit. And those who upset law and order, that disciplinary measures be taken against them and, if need be, to eliminate them from our units. So at all briefings and all my contacts with the Military Police Administration also told us that anybody who besmirched the name of the military police on battlegrounds throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they should be thrown out of the units." [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd also like to invite you to pay your attention to document P3571. Valentin Coric had the following to say concerning a case of rape of two Muslim girls by military policemen: "The named persons defamed the military police, and their further retention in the unit would be detrimental." The entire case file is handed over to the competent Military Prosecutor's Office. I'd like to move on to my next topic. In their final brief, the Prosecution asserted that Valentin Coric established and controlled check-points throughout Herceg-Bosna, using them in order to control movement, and to render delivery of international assistance, including humanitarian assistance, impossible. They seek to corroborate this thesis of theirs in paragraphs 1000 to 1015 of their final brief. Your Honours, not a single document the Prosecutor referred to in those paragraphs proves that Valentin Coric in any way disrupted the movement of humanitarian organisations as well as their lending assistance. Also, contrary to the Prosecution thesis, these documents show that Valentin Coric had no exclusive authority over check-points. The military police didn't have any either. The Coric Defence, in our final brief in paragraphs 324 to 337, dealt with the topic of check-points. Therefore, in this presentation I will simply briefly comment on certain allegations made by the Prosecutor. In paragraph 1000, the Prosecutor asserts that Petkovic, in his order number P1673, confirmed that the military police was responsible for roads. This document shows only that Petkovic did order the military police without informing the Military Police Administration about this order, as the assertion stands. The Coric Defence asserts that the check-points were not manned by military policemen and that the personnel at those check-points were not under the control of the Military Police Administration. This is shown in document P1548, which shows that operational zone commanders commanded the check-points through their brigade commanders. Also, in addition to military policemen, those check-points were manned by soldiers. Both were commanded by operational zone commanders. The Prosecutor puts forth document P1331 as a key example of Coric's order, proving that Coric controlled entry to Mostar. The only thing you can see on the basis of that document is that it came about due to a deteriorating security situation, and that because of that, searches of persons, vehicles, and cargo were ordered. There is no mention whatsoever of any ban on movement of international assistance or international organisations. This order was issued based on an order of the commander of the South-East Herzegovina Operational Zone, which is document P1272. In the order, he clearly states that it was being issued because there were check-points formed inside the town without the knowledge of the Command of South-Eastern Herzegovina Operational Zone, and because armed groups appeared, threatening the security of all, as well as because of the attack on a police check-point in Grabovica. Document P1134, referred to by the Prosecutor in paragraph 1001, also has nothing to do with humanitarian assistance or with international agencies. It is specifically mentioned that Valentin Coric did not personally sign the document, because at the time he was not in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is something we discussed in our final brief in paragraph 625. The Prosecutor also refers to document P1654, P1654. Your Honours, this document also has nothing to do with humanitarian assistance or with representatives of the international organisations. It is clear from the document that its author focused his attention on law and public order and the prevention of crime. The last sentence of the document clearly indicates that the operational zone commanded the military police in the town of Mostar. In order to corroborate their thesis, the Prosecution referred to document P1868, the so-called plan of increased control of the town of Mostar. The Coric Defence, first and foremost, wishes to stress that it is clear from the document that the plan was drafted jointly by some other organs, including the command of the operational zone, and not the Military Police Administration or its head. It is clear, on the basis of the document, that a dedicated task force was put together, on whose behalf Lavric signed the plan. Therefore, Lavric did not sign the document about this plan as Coric's deputy. It doesn't say that in the document either. He signed this on his own behalf and on behalf of the task force. All important telephone numbers are specified in the document, including the telephone numbers of the chief of the Main Staff, the commander of the operational zone, the deputy commander of the operational zone, as well as commanders of certain military police units. However, Your Honours, there is no number that would be Valentin Coric's number. Also, at the end of the document, there is a list of people who were supposed to receive the document. Next to the name of each body specified, we have a specific person that was to receive the plan; for example, to the operational zone commander, to the Police Administration and its head, to the head of the Department of Internal Affairs. Your Honours, there is nothing written next to the "Military Police Administration," no functional title, no name. The Coric Defence asserts that there is no evidence that Coric was part of this plan or that he was acquainted with it. The Coric Defence furthermore asserts that a few days following the document, Valentin Coric issued an order on the establishment of joint police patrols between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO, following an order issued by the commander of the South-Eastern Herzegovina Operational Zone commander. This is indicated in documents P2030 and P2020. The documents referred to by the Prosecutor in paragraph 1004, there is no mention of the military police. In paragraph 1006, the Prosecution states that the military police, during the siege of Mostar, prevented international organisations from entering Mostar. They refer to several documents, of which not one refers to the military police. By the same token, they also invoke an adjudicated fact, which also makes no reference to the military police. Your Honours, the Coric Defence asserts that out of all of the evidence referred to by the Prosecutor, none of them show that Coric was in any way controlling the check-points or that the military police was the one preventing the distribution of humanitarian assistance. This is further corroborated by the evidence presented by this Defence. The Coric Defence asserts that the freedom of movement in a particular area was decided upon solely by military commanders in their respective areas of responsibility. It is visible, from documents P2108, P2461, P2531, P2680, P4027, and P4623 that various military commanders met from various levels, starting with the chief of the Main Staff and other people from the Main Staff, as well as different commanders from the Command of the Operational Zone of South-East Herzegovina, as well as commanders of local brigades. They met 27 times in total in order to negotiate with the international organisations or with their mediation concerning the issue of the freedom of movement. All these meetings and talks took place between the 26th of April, 1993, and the 2nd of September, 1993. All the documents I listed are documents of representatives of international organisations. Your Honours, neither Valentin Coric nor anyone else from the Military Police Administration or military police was present at any of these negotiations. As for the freedom of movement, I direct your attention to the following documents: P2421, P6825, P3923, P3895, P3835 and P5104. Your Honours, a protected witness testified here, a representative of an international organisations, DZ. His statement is admitted as P10367. Just in case, I wish us to move to private session just for two minutes.

utterances.text: We are in open session. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] The Petkovic Defence, in paragraph 387 of its final brief, deals with snipers in the Mostar area in the relevant period, as they say, between the 30th of June until the 24th of July, and claims that the Prosecution failed to prove that in this period, civilians were targeted by snipers who belonged to the regular HVO forces. It is noted in footnote 690 that the HVO military police also had snipers in its units, thus insinuating that they were the ones who may have targeted civilians. In this, the Petkovic Defence refers to the semi-annual report of the Military Police Administration for the first half of 1993. Your Honours, this semi-annual report for the first half of 1993 is the sole document which connects the Military Police Administration in any way whatsoever with snipers. As for snipers, the document only says that the Military Police Administration organised sniper training and that the result of sniper combat after the training is 6:1. Your Honours, there is nothing bad in training snipers, particularly not training which included the Geneva Conventions and which was organised and implemented by the Military Police Administration. And likewise, Your Honours, sniper combat does not mean targeting civilians, but rather combat among the snipers. In response to the claims made by the Petkovic Defence, the Coric Defence, first of all, wishes to say that this document does not relate to the period for which the Petkovic Defence claims it is relevant, that is to say, the period between the 30th of June and the 24th of July, but rather to an earlier period. Further, the Coric Defence would like to remind Your Honours that General Praljak, testifying before this Tribunal, confirmed that the snipers in Mostar belonged to the 2nd Brigade of the HVO, which is recorded on the following transcript pages: 42892 through to 42898. The Coric Defence also invites Your Honours to examine document P1307. It is a document dated the 26th of January, 1993. It is an order from the chief of Main Staff, which says: "Due to the newly-arisen situation, it is necessary to collect urgently 40 sniper rifles as follows: Citluk, 10; Grude, 10; Ljubuski, 10; Siroki Brijeg, 10. The dead-line for carrying out this order is the 26th of January. The rifles, with listed numbers, shall be submitted by the said dead-line to the Main Staff of the Mostar HVO. If necessary, also engage military police for the collection of rifles." The document was sent to the South-Eastern Herzegovina Operational Zone, the 4th Brigade of the HVO in Ljubuski, the Citluk Battalion, Ljubuski, Grude, Siroki Brijeg Battalion. Your Honours, the Coric Defence claims that there is no evidence that Valentin Coric is responsible for incidents connected with civilians being targeted by snipers in Mostar. We'll now move to our next topic. In its closing arguments, the Prosecution alleges that the Military Police Administration participated in illegal moving in into the apartments from which the earlier tenants were previously evicted by force, and these tenants were ethnic Muslims, and refers to documents P2879 and P6232. Document P2879, which the Prosecution refers to, does not show that these were Muslim apartments. Likewise, it does not show what were the dates at which members of military police moved into these apartments, whether that happened in 1993 or whether it could have taken place in 1992. During 1992, many Serbs left Mostar, and they made up almost 20 per cent of the population, and, therefore, they had at their disposal a proportionate segment of the housing stock. In addition to that, there were also many apartments which used to belong to the JNA and which, according to the decree, were placed at the disposal of the municipal authorities, which is testified to by the document 1D03016. In addition to that, the document that the Prosecution refers to does not show that the apartments were forcibly occupied. Likewise, document P62332 does not show that these were apartments from which their previous users were forcibly evicted, nor can this be seen from any other document. The Decree on the Use of Abandoned Apartments, dating from July 1993, which is document P03089, Article 2 defines what is to be considered as an abandoned apartment, and Article 1 states when the right to use the apartment expires for the previous tenancy rights holder. Article 7 notes the conditions under which an apartment, for which it was established by a decision that it can be considered abandoned, can be given for use to a member of HVO or a person who, due to actions caused by war, was left without his or her apartment. The temporary use of an apartment may last up to one year from the day of the termination of immediate threat of war. Article 9 of this decree says that the body of the municipal HVO administration in charge of housing issues is the body which gives an abandoned apartment for use. Before this decree, the municipal authorities would adopt regulations on their own by which they established the manner of temporary use of apartments, as testified by the documents 1D01127, 1D03016, 1D00435, 1D00717, and 1D1152. The issue of military apartments was regulated by a decree on the temporary use of military apartments. It follows from this that in both documents which the Prosecution refers to in its closing arguments, the Military Police Administration acted in accordance with the procedure as prescribed by the quoted decree. It would submit a request to the relevant body, and the subject of the requests were the apartments which were covered by the conditions noted in this decree. Additionally, we note that Rade Lavric, for whom the Prosecution also says that he signed the above two documents on behalf of the Military Police Administration, held the position of president for control and monitoring of the use of military apartments at the level of the South-Eastern Herzegovina Operational Zone, in which a housing commission was formed and chaired by Stipe Maric. We note that the housing commission submitted reports to the commander of the South-Eastern Herzegovina Operational Zone. An example of such a report is P6860. In the report, the chairman of the commission says that the military police shall evict all persons who illegally moved into such apartments, that is to say, all those who do not have a decision permitting them to use these apartments and which was issued to them by the said commission. We can see from all this that the Prosecution claim, from the closing arguments, about the greediness of the military police for Muslim apartments, is only insulting and nothing more. The existence of abandoned apartments is the subject of decreed laws, and the fact that someone submitted a request to be issued a decision on temporary use of those apartments, in accordance with the legal regulations which were then in force, does not justify anyone to draw a conclusion that the previous tenants were evicted by force from these precise apartments and that these were automatically criminal acts. Abandoned apartments were allocated to members of various HVO units; for example, documents P2538 and P2608 talk about this. Likewise, the municipal HVO authorities allocated apartments to Muslims who met the criteria set out in the decree; for example, P3444 and 1D641 show that. Additionally, the Coric Defence notes that such practice of allocating abandoned apartments to certain categories of military officials and expellees and refugees, based on the same legal institutes using apartments which were abandoned by their previous users without a valid basis, was something that was also applied in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as seen from document 3D734. The basis for acting in the organs of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was the relevant decree law on abandoned apartments, and that is document 1D530. I still owe you the number of the decree on the temporary use of abandoned apartments. That is P1384. The decree was issued on the 1st of February, 1993. I'm moving on to a new topic. In their closing argument, the Prosecution said that Mr. Coric contributed to the joint criminal enterprise by approving and subscribing to the administrative system of deportations, according to which detainees could be released from prisons on a condition that together with their families, they left Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Coric Defence already dealt with the matter in their final brief, so today I'm going to refer only to what Mr. Stringer said in his closing argument. Your Honours, most of the presentation from now on will be concerning a protected witness, so can we go into private session to protect the witness?

TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, in their closing arguments, asserted that the Coric Defence, in our final brief, disputed the authenticity of document P3220 solely based on the allegation of a forged signature. This is incorrect. Your Honours, the Valentin Coric Defence, in paragraph 699 to 702, disputes the authenticity of documents P3220 and P3216. In both these documents, there's an alleged response by Valentin Coric to an order issued by Colonel Nedjeljko Obradovic. It is clear, on the basis of the document, that it was sent to the prison wardens in Gabela, Dretelj, Heliodrom, and Ljubuski. The Coric Defence, in our final brief, put forth a number of reasons due to which we believe this document is a counterfeit. I will only mention a few. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor, in their closing arguments, imply that Colonel Obradovic did not have real authority at Heliodrom. The Coric Defence dealt with Colonel Obradovic and his authority over prisons in detail in our final brief. Therefore, I will specify but one example here. On the 8th of July, 1993, Valentin Coric approved for UNHCR representatives to visit the prisons of Dretelj, Ljubuski, and Heliodrom. The document number is P3292. On the 10th of July, UNHCR representatives, together with a representative of the ODPR, visited the Heliodrom. During the visit, Mr. Herceg told the UNHCR representatives that the ODPR was responsible for the civilians and that the HVO was responsible for the detainees. During that visit, the UNHCR, together with the ODPR, visited the persons accommodated in the gym and the school building. As for the detainees, they were told that they were in the prison building which was also at the Heliodrom. The ODPR representative, as well as the military officials present during that occasion, informed the UNHCR that the International Committee of the Red Cross had visited the prison building previously. It was because of that and some other reasons that UNHCR did not insist on visiting the prison themselves. Beside that, UNHCR was also told that no repeated visits were granted to the ICRC, following which UNHCR withdrew. It is all seen in document P9843. Both documents were referred to by the Prosecution in their final brief, and the Prlic Defence also invited the Chamber to view the documents. Your Honours, in the approval issued by Valentin Coric, there were no restrictions contained. He didn't specify which buildings were open to access and which were not. He simply approved that prison visit. I'd like to draw your attention to document 5D3008 to that end. It concerns a meeting called by Colonel Obradovic on the 6th of July, 1993, with his subordinates in attendance. That was a few days before the visit at the Heliodrom. Among other people, there were also representatives of the 3rd Brigade present at the meeting, and the 3rd Brigade was located at the Heliodrom. The commander of the military police company located in the barracks in Dretelj was also present. On that occasion, Colonel Obradovic provided instructions for the work in prisons, and among other things, he prohibited access to all international organisations to the Heliodrom. Your Honours, as we could see in document P3292, Valentin Coric, without restriction, approved the visit of the representatives of international organisations in order to visit the detainees at the Heliodrom, in Dretelj, and in Ljubuski. Still, at the Heliodrom, that approval was not taken into account. Why not? Because Obradovic, on the 6th of July, prohibited any international organisations' visits. Your Honours, in paragraph 193 of the indictment, the OTP assert that until August, international organisations failed to enter Dretelj. Your Honour, Valentin Coric issued his approval to go to Dretelj as early as the 8th of July. Only two conclusions can be drawn from this. First, Valentin Coric in no way hindered access to international organisations to prisons and detainees. Second, Valentin Coric was not a person of authority, be it at Dretelj or at the Heliodrom. The Coric Defence submits that the de facto authority in all prisons in Sector South, including the Heliodrom, lay with Colonel Obradovic, who was the sector commander. In paragraph 213 of their final brief, the Petkovic Defence stated that any army obligations vis-a-vis the prisoners cease at the moment of their hand-over to the Department of Defence, including the military police. The Coric Defence submit that military commanders never handed over those prisoners to the Military Police Administration. When the military police take part in providing security of POWs or conducts internal security of military prisons, such tasks fall under regular daily tasks, and in such situations the military police is under the command of the operational zone commander. I discussed that and the system of command for the military police. Therefore, there is no need for me to repeat myself today. In addition to that, the Coric Defence submits that the military commanders never surrendered their authority to any other organ over the persons they had taken prisoner or arrested. It was the military commanders who decided on their fate. Your Honours, if we look at the documents issued by international observers, P2108, P2461, P2512, P2531, P2547, P2675, and P2680 we see that various senior military commanders, in the periods between May and September 1993, participated in different talks and meetings 14 times. The release and exchanges of prisoners were discussed at those meetings. However, at those meetings, no one from the Military Police Administration was present. At those meetings, those commanders did not declare themselves unauthorised or incompetent to negotiate. The military commanders decided on the exchanges and release of prisoners. They had the lists of those who were taken prisoner, and they decided on their fate. Your Honour, I'd like to draw your attention to the document P2108 issued by the international observers. At page 38, it reads that the lists of all detainees at the Heliodrom, as of the 18th of August, 1993, were handed over to that international organisation by Zarko Keza. Your Honours, he is a member of the Military Intelligence Service of the Main Staff. While we're on the topic of prisoner lists: The Prosecution, in paragraph 1089 of their final brief, assert that Valentin Coric was informed that on the 9th of May, at the Heliodrom, there were civilians who had been arrested. They refer to a list from that document. It is clear, by perusing the document, that the Military Police Administration received that document as late as the 22nd of June, 1993; that is to say, a full month after those persons had already left the Heliodrom. Valentin Coric and the Military Police Administration did not decide on the arrival and departure of those people to and from the Heliodrom. Not only that, but the Military Police Administration received the list a full month later, after everything had been over. Regarding who took over prisoners after they were taken prisoner, and who were they handed over to de facto, I wish to quote the page transcript 51323 and 51324. It is the testimony of Witness NO. For that person, I'd like to ask that we go into closed session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] In connection with this topic, the Coric Defence directs Your Honours' attention to the following documents: P1959, in which the commander of the Main Staff orders that the exchange of all prisoners begin at once, this order he addresses to operational zones; document P1351, which shows that the commander of the operational zone and the commander of the brigade have lists of those who were taken prisoner and are deciding on the exchanges; document P3958 is the number of prisoners in Dretelj, addressed to the brigade; document 4D347, order of the operational zone commander, addressed to all his units, to release arrested civilians; document P1994, Main Staff commander orders all operational zones how they are to treat arrested civilians and soldiers, telling them that they must report the identity of all prisoners to the ICRC and enable the ICRC to visit the prisoners; P4156, the brigade commander issues an order relating to the accommodation and living conditions for prisoners of war. The Military Police Administration did not decide on the release or exchange of prisoners. At the request of relevant bodies, the Military Police Crime Investigation Department provided information whether criminal proceedings were being conducted against the person or not. Documents P4379, 6D169, and P4450 show this. Your Honours, the International Committee of the Red Cross addressed high-ranking military commanders on a number of occasions concerning the issue of treatment of prisoners of war, including forced labour. They also addressed Mr. Petkovic among these. None of them ever told the International Committee of the Red Cross to address the Military Police Administration, nor that the Military Police Administration was responsible for the treatment of prisoners. In connection with this, Your Honours, please review the following documents: P284, P2950, P7629, P7636, P7660, P5308, and P5967. Why am I saying this? Because in its final brief, the Prosecution uses, as the only documents that connect the Military Police Administration with forced labour, the following documents: P4020 and P4030. The former is a document signed by Mr. Petkovic, which says that the Military Police Administration is responsible for the use of prisoners, and the latter document is a document from the Posusje Brigade, which supposedly acts on Mr. Petkovic's instructions and requests prisoners for labour from, as the document says, the VPHB Coric. Document P4068 is a report of the brigade military police from the very same Posusje Brigade, which says that they acted on the request from the brigade and took the prisoners from the Otok Prison. Your Honours, there is no evidence that Valentin Coric or anyone else from the Military Police Administration ever received or saw any of these three documents, nor that anyone from the Military Police Administration or Valentin Coric ever acted on this request. Concerning these two documents which are connected with the Posusje Brigade, the Defence particularly points out something else that is illogical. The Posusje Brigade is located in the North-Western Herzegovina Operational Zone. The Otok Prison was located in the South-Eastern Herzegovina Operational Zone. It is not logical that the Posusje Brigade, when the war operations were in full swing, should come to fetch prisoners for labour from the North-Western Herzegovina Operational Zone to another operational zone, particularly when, at the same time in the area of the North-Western Herzegovina Operational Zone, there were prisoners which were under the control of the Prozor Brigade and the joint commander of all brigades in this area, Mr. Siljeg, from the North-Western Herzegovina Operational Zone. And there are documents which show that. Now I will just say a few short remarks on the subject of prison from the Prosecution final brief. In paragraph 1071, the Prosecution, in order to prove that Valentin Coric established the rules of conduct at the Ljubuski Prison, refers to document P234. Your Honours, document P234 is a document from a prison in Croatia, the Kerestinac Prison. This document has really nothing to do with Ljubuski, nor with the HVO military police, nor with the HVO Military Police Administration, except that an unidentified person scribbled on the document, crossed out words, and added other words such as, for example, "Ljubuski" and "Valentin Coric." The document has not been shown to any witness, nor is there any other piece of evidence that would connect this document with the Ljubuski Prison. Paragraph 1161 of the Prosecution's final brief says that on the 23rd of September, 1993, the Muslim civilians tried to prevent the transfer of prisoners who were being sent from Dretelj to Croatia. The Prosecution refers to document P5322. Your Honours, this document does not deal with Muslim civilians. These were not the Muslim civilians who were protesting. The Croats were protesting, Croats who tried to prevent the release of these prisoners from the prison. This was confirmed by Prosecution Witness C. In connection with this, the Defence refers Your Honours to paragraphs 590 and 591 of its final brief. The Coric Defence claims that Valentin Coric never, not even after the incidents on the 30th of June, 1993, issued an order on disarming, arresting, or isolating Muslim members of the HVO. The Coric Defence claims that according to the information which Valentin Coric had at his disposal, he knew about the attack of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina launched on the 30th of June, 1993, and the role of Muslim members of the HVO in this attack. After the 30th of June, 1993, within the military police, and due to this security situation, a security check of military policemen of Muslim ethnicity was carried out, and that was repeated in the fall of 1993, but not a single Muslim from the military police was arrested or interned. The Military Police Administration assessed that this was not necessary. According to the information that could have reached the Military Police Administration, Valentin Coric could only have known that the military commanders in the Capljina and Stolac areas disarmed and isolated the Muslim members of their units and able-bodied Muslims. Valentin Coric had no reason to doubt the legitimacy of the decision of these military commanders because they were in the position to best know what the security situation in their units was, as well as in their zone of responsibility. In addition to this, Valentin Coric believed, judging by himself and the Military Police Administration, that everyone else acted in the same manner. In particular, I direct Your Honours' attention to document P3960. The interpreters have it. The Coric Defence a few weeks ago requested the Prosecution to provide a corrected translation of this document. However, to this day we only received the answer that this was in procedure. We have provided the Croatian text to the interpreter's booth from which I will read only one single sentence which is underlined for the sake of the interpreters. It's a report personally to Valentin Coric, addressed by the commander of the 5th Battalion of the Military Police, and the date is the 5th of August, 1993 : "The order on arresting members of Muslim ethnicity for preventive reasons made great difficulty and problems for us." Your Honours, in the translation that the Coric Defence objected against, which is the reason why we insisted that the translation be corrected, lacked the word "preventive," and it is obvious that in the Croatian text, this word exists. Your Honours, at the moment when Valentin Coric learned what the actual situation in Dretelj was, according to the testimony of Witness C on transcript page 22381 and 22382, and that was a Prosecution witness, in July Valentin Coric brought Ivan Ancic, the then commander of the Military Police Company in Dretelj, to a government session so that he would inform the government about what was going on in Dretelj. We know that the government session was held on the 19th of July, 1993, and we know that a commission which was to check the situation was sent to Capljina and Stolac. Your Honours, in spite of all the effort made, the government was powerless here. After that, in September 1993, at the Collegium of the Defence Department, it was precisely Valentin Coric who warned, once again, about poor practice in running prisons. Eventually, on the 15th of September, 1993, Mate Boban issued an order requesting that all norms of International Law and Geneva Conventions should be observed in detention centres. Mate Boban, in item 7 of this order, requests the Main Staff to inform all subordinate units and commands with this order, and that the Main Staff should help all these units to implement the order. Mate Boban requested the Main Staff to implement the order. He did not request the Defence Department or the Military Police Administration to do that. The document in question is P5104. Your Honours, the Coric Defence, due to limitations of time, is unable, in its closing arguments, to address all topics connected with prisons. What we have presented here is just a shorter version of what is included in our final brief in paragraphs 338 through to 609. Your Honours, the Coric Defence invites Your Honours to check very cautiously and with due attention every allegation of the Prosecution from their final brief and compare it with the evidence which are offered to corroborate these allegations. There are good reasons, and the Coric Defence is not saying this just so. So far through our presentation, we have showed documents which have been wrongly interpreted or contents was added to them which the documents do not include. Unfortunately, the Defence does not have enough time to point out each and every one of such documents, but we direct Your Honours' attention, for example, to paragraph 1143 of the Prosecution final brief, in which it is claimed that the military police participated in an incident, whereas the quotation from the witness testimony that the Prosecution refers to just says the HVO police. Your Honours, it is a well-known fact that the HVO had both military and civilian police. The witness was here, and the Prosecutor should have, could have, and indeed had to ask the witness which police this was, but the Prosecution did not do that, and it's their problem. In paragraph 1150, the Prosecution claims that Witness BJ said that the military police was involved in the mass transfer of Muslim civilians from Grude to Ljubuski. The Prosecution also refers to document P3744. Your Honours, the document does not say what the Prosecution claims, and Witness BJ, on transcript pages 5819 and 5820 during cross-examination, said that he did not know at all which persons these were or where these persons were going or why. The witness was unable to say whether these were Muslims, or Croats, or anything. Your Honours, the Coric Defence claims that several documents in this case are forgeries. It has claimed so during this presentation and also in its final brief. In case of such arguments of Defence, the Prosecution took the stand which implies that such a situation is impossible, particularly if a document has the stamp from archives, and that the Defence makes such objections just because such documents do not fit its purpose. The Prosecution takes this stand even though it claimed itself that it was facing the same problem a few years ago. Even the book about the former Chief Prosecutor of this Tribunal deals with the same issue. Your Honours, the Prosecution of this Tribunal submitted a request for a reconsideration of judgement in Blaskic case. This is to be found in the judicial database of this Tribunal and can be accessed by everyone. In this request, the Prosecution claimed that the appeals judgement in the Blaskic case was founded on an at least strange document of a state organ of the Republic of Croatia; namely, there were two versions of one-and-the-same document. One of them had 20 pages, the other one 40 pages. The longer version contained the name of the source from whom the information on incidents relating to Ahmici was obtained, including information on the dual chain of command as regards military police in Central Bosnia. The source of all this information was Mr. Blaskic's Defence attorney, Mr. Nobilo. This is what the longer version of the document says. However, what was submitted to the Trial Chamber was the abbreviated version, the shorter version, that had only 20 pages and from which the information about the source of information was left out, so it turned out that the state organ learned everything through operative work from impartial sources. It was precisely on the basis of the new information that the appeals judgement in the Blaskic case was passed. It was precisely on the basis of this information that the myth about the dual chain of command of military police came into being. Your Honours, Valentin Coric's Defence claims that Valentin Coric is not guilty and that the Prosecution has not proved beyond reasonable doubt that he's guilty, and, therefore, asks Your Honours to acquit Valentin Coric on all counts of the indictment. I have finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam. You have adhered to the time, and now we can move on to Mr. Pusic's Defence. Mr. Pusic is absent due to illness. He is represented by his counsel. I would like to give the floor to the first speaker who is going to address the Trial Chamber on behalf of Mr. Berislav Pusic. You have the floor, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You should approach considerably to the microphone. Otherwise, you are hard to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: It may also help if I turn the microphone on, Your Honour, which I have. Your Honours, I'll start again. Even in the most complicated and lengthy of criminal trials, of which this is one, trials of this nature often turn on one or two relatively narrow issues once all the other extraneous facts are stripped away. In this particular case, in respect of Mr. Pusic, we have identified two issues. The first issue is whether, in a high-level leadership trial, such as this, where none of the accused are said to have directly participated in any crimes, the issue is whether the evidence proves beyond reasonable doubt that Mr. Pusic had any decision-making powers. Our second issue follows from that. Assuming that our first submission is accepted and that the Chamber find that Mr. Pusic is not a direct perpetrator of any crimes and that he had no decision-making powers, then, Your Honours, should he be held criminally responsible for any of the offences on the indictment? We will frame our submissions today around these two questions. Your Honours, we hope that our Defence is crystal clear from the very opening of our brief. Our defence is that the Prosecution have failed to prove that Mr. Pusic had any decision-making powers, they failed to prove that beyond reasonable doubt, and that, accordingly, he should be acquitted of all the charges on the indictment. You have indicated, Your Honours, that the purpose of closing submissions, as far as you are concerned, is for the parties to answer the arguments that have been raised both in writing and orally. I would like to turn to some of the arguments that were advanced by the Prosecution in the course of their closing submissions. The Prosecution began their closing submissions in respect of Mr. Pusic by stating that the Pusic Defence faced a number of dilemmas. Madam Registrar, could I ask for the Sanction facility to be switched on. And, Your Honours, we have a PowerPoint presentation. The first slide that we would like to present to you is an extract of the submissions made by Mr. Kruger. It appears we're having some technical problems. I hope they can be resolved. So, Your Honours, during the course of submissions by the Prosecution, there were two assertions made. The first, and I will quote, although I don't intend to quote from all the slides that I will be presenting in the course of my address to you today, but I quote: "And that brings us to the third dilemma. Pusic's claim that he had no power and authority is not based on any evidence, because he's put none before the Court. It is based only on the bare assertions of Pusic in his final trial brief." And at some point later in the Prosecution's submissions, it was stated that: "The Prosecution respectfully submits that Mr. Pusic's simple assertions of his innocence, unsupported by any sworn testimony or alternative evidence from him, is not sufficient to overcome these dilemmas." Your Honours, we submit that those remarks display a misunderstanding of the burden of proof, and we will address you in due course on that particular subject. And, Your Honours, it is, of course, the case that Mr. Pusic did not testify in this trial, that the Pusic Defence did not call any witnesses. It is Mr. Pusic's right not to call witnesses, his right not to testify, a right that's enshrined in law, and we would ask you not to draw any adverse inferences from his exercise of that right. The point that we would like to emphasise is that our submissions on behalf of the Defence rests not just on bare assertions made by Mr. Pusic's lawyers, but they rest on an analysis of the evidence that has been called by the Prosecution. Importantly, we say that this is a case where the Prosecution witnesses gave evidence that could be interpreted to support our defence. And, Your Honours, I would like to begin by referring you to the evidence of three of the witnesses called by the Prosecution, three important witnesses. The first witness, Marijan Biskic. And may I apologise, Your Honours, if I mispronounce any of the names in this case, and I do have problems pronouncing the -- I'm sorry, I do have problems with the pronunciation of the names in this region, Your Honour. The lack of vowels and preponderance of consonants does cause me sometimes to stumble over the correct pronunciation. But Mr. Biskic, he said that: "He, Pusic, could not issue an order to me or to anybody else, I believe." Quite unequivocal. Biskic is an important witness, somebody who was familiar not only with Pusic's work, but also with the internal mechanics of the HVO. The Prosecution called him. He was their witness. They didn't challenge him on this or any other aspect of his evidence, and they called him as a witness of truth. Your Honours, I will turn to the evidence of this particular witness in due course. The second important witness we would ask you to consider - and, Madam Registrar, perhaps we could just go into private session for a few moments -- is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: We submit that the analysis of these three witnesses can be fairly applied to every spear of activity that Mr. Pusic was involved in. Your Honours, and we don't need to remind you, as professional judges, that the Defence in this case don't have to prove anything. All we have to show is that there is another reasonable inference available from the evidence. And given the evidence of these three witnesses, given their testimony, we ask you to consider if the inference that Pusic had no unilateral decision-making power can be simply set aside and discarded. We submit if you cannot set aside/discard the testimony of these three witnesses, then it follows -- it follows that there must be a reasonable inference that Pusic, in the words of Biskic, could not give orders to him or to anyone else. And, Your Honours, I also echo the words of Mr. Khan, who was standing where I'm standing a few days ago, and remind him of what he said to you, which is that, If there is any doubt in your minds, that doubt must be exercised in favour of the accused. Your Honour, we go further than just to say that we've raised a reasonable doubt. We submit that if you -- even if you are trying this case on a different standard, if you are trying this case on a balance of probabilities, we'd submit that you could find the facts, as interpreted by us, as presented by the Prosecution, support an alternative theory, and they support the theory that Pusic was a low-level civil servant who had no decision-making authority. Your Honours, given that the purpose of these closing addresses at the end of a five-year trial are for all parties to refer to the relevant arguments advanced in written submissions, you may have found it surprising that the evidence of these three witnesses, which is fairly prominently highlighted in our final trial brief, was not extensively referred to by the Prosecution in the course of their oral submissions. We suggest that that is an omission -- a glaring omission that can only be explained in one way. The Prosecution failed to address this evidence because they can't explain it, because they realise that these points represent an Achilles heel in their case, and that's why they seek either to evade or ignore it. Your Honours, I hope you have before you an outline of our submissions today. In the remainder of my speech, I will move on to consider what we suggest to be serious legal errors made by the Prosecution in the course of their closing submissions to you. We'll then outline some general points in the nature of our defence before dealing with the evidence against Mr. Pusic. And I turn to deal with the evidence related to Mr. Pusic within the framework of the two questions that I outlined to you in the course of my introduction. We'll then move on, Your Honours, to look at the question of Article 7(3), command responsibility, before examining issues of JCE liability, and then sentencing remarks will follow. In the course of the submissions made by the Prosecution last week, one of the main accusations made was that the Defence had been highly selective in their use of quotes. Your Honours, my view on this really originates, and my interest in this trial originates, on the international criminal justice system, from my initial studies as a historian. And my first degree was in history and politics, and one of the first texts that I was asked to read as a history student was a treatise on histography by a British author called E.H. Carr. And he said, in a characteristically provocative way, that: "The belief in a hardcore of historical facts existing objectively and independently of the interpretation of the historian is a preposterous fallacy, but one which it is very hard to eradicate." Your Honours, I take the view that one can attempt to be objective, one can attempt to take the reasoned and fair view of the evidence, while still coming to a firm conclusion, but it is inevitable that in the course of any analysis, legal or historical, that there will be some criticism that could be laid of selectivity. Bearing this in mind, it is apparent from our final trial brief that we have had the luxury -- we have been in the position where we have had the luxury of being able to quote extensively from the relevant witnesses. And, Your Honours, I would like to emphasise that we have done so for one simple reason, and that is because we have endeavoured to make sure there can be no doubt as to what was actually entered in the evidence during the course of this trial. And, Your Honours, the Pusic Defence does not accept the Prosecution's criticism that we have simply ignored incriminating material. If you examine paragraphs 120 and 126 of our final trial brief, you will see that we have addressed various aspects of the testimony of Witness DZ that do not entirely advance the Pusic Defence, and in due course, if there is a rebuttal, if the Prosecution do choose to address the points that we have raised today, it may well be that the Prosecutor chooses to highlight other remarks made by DZ to ridicule the submissions made by the Defence. Well, that is part and parcel of adversarial proceedings. We would respectfully ask the Chamber to focus on DZ's evidence in the round, to take the rough with the smooth, because, in our submission, it's quite clear that if you do that, it's quite clear that Witness DZ considered Pusic not to be one of the main players in the HVO and not to have any decision-making powers. In the same spirit, we would ask the Chamber to examine the evidence of all the international experts who testified against Mr. Pusic in the round, to look at their evidence globally, because it's simply not possible to reconcile what certain witnesses, Witness BB, BC and BD, say, to reconcile that with the testimony of international witnesses DZ and DV. And where there are contradictions, we suggest that the Trial Chamber should give preference and weight to those witnesses who had regular direct contact with Mr. Pusic, whose evidence is based on their first-hand experience and not on unattributed hearsay. And, Your Honours, that is a submission that we develop in more detail in paragraphs 110 to 112 of our final brief. In summary, we also say this: that if you do come to the conclusion that the Pusic Defence has misstated or misinterpreted the evidence against Mr. Pusic, then please do not hold it against Mr. Pusic. Ultimately, Your Honours, we recognise that it's up to you to decide whether the conclusions that we've drawn from what we say is an exhaustive and careful review of all the material, if those conclusions are fair, balanced, and justified, but we would ask, furthermore, that the Chamber treat the submissions that have been advanced by the Prosecution and the Defence to the same degree and level of scrutiny. We have tried to be transparent with the Trial Chamber. We stand by every word of our final trial brief, and we say that we have presented you with a scenario that is far closer to the truth than that advanced by the Prosecution. Your Honours, at the beginning of my speech, I referred to an extract from the Prosecution's closing submissions concerning statements misstating the law relating to the burden of proof. And, Your Honours, there are three legal errors in the Prosecution's opening submissions that we would like to explore with you now. The first relates to that very issue, the burden of proof. During the course of their closing argument, there were three statements that were made that we take issue with. The first: The Prosecution said, and I paraphrase, that the Pusic Defence has presented no evidence whatsoever that could convince the Trial Chamber to come to a different conclusion. That's at transcript page 52140. They went on to say: "Pusic put the Prosecution to proof and responded with a passive and silent defence." Transcript page 52161. And then, and perhaps of most concern is the following: "The problem for Mr. Pusic is his silent and passive defence. He did not provide the Chamber with any evidence to support his interpretation. The Trial Chamber has only his unsworn and untested word in the form of his final brief and perhaps his earlier 98 bis submissions." Your Honours, obvious point that arises from that, the Defence do not have to prove anything, and that's one point that the common law and civil law jurisdictions often have in common. In France, it's recognised in Article 9 of the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, and in some national jurisdictions -- in the United States -- in parts of the United States, for instance, I understand that any criticism of the Defence for not testifying, for not calling evidence, would be entirely prohibited and would be immediate grounds for a mistrial on the basis that it violates a citizen's 5th Amendment rights. So, Your Honours, it's regrettable you can't trust the Prosecution to accurately state and apply the law. As far as it concerns the Defence, these are basic principles of the Tribunal's jurisprudence. Your Honours, the Prosecution also described another dilemma they said faced the Pusic Defence, and it was stated thus : "The first dilemma for the Pusic Defence, Your Honours, is that the Pusic Defence has already presented all of their current arguments to the Chamber previously during their 98 bis submissions in January 2008." And that's transcript reference 52139. Your Honours, that assertion is patently incorrect. The arguments that were presented on behalf of Mr. Pusic during the 98 bis submission did not address the strengths and weaknesses of the evidence against him in any respect. In our 98 bis submissions, we simply asserted that there was no evidence linking Mr. Pusic to Counts 4, 5, and 19 to 26 inclusive of the indictment, and there was no evidence linking him to other specified allegations within other individual counts. And, Your Honour, this is a submission that you'll find developed in more detail in Part 2 of our final trial brief at paragraphs 32 to 36. The remainder of our submissions focus on the law and, in particular, a discussion of JCE 3 liability. Your Honours, the third error made by the Prosecution during the course of their 98 bis submissions arises from what we say is a fundamental misunderstanding of the test set out in Rule 98 bis. The Prosecution said that the Defence faced another dilemma because, as a consequence of the Chamber's 98 bis finding -- Your Honour, I'll quote directly: "Since that time, Your Honours, the Pusic Defence has not placed any alternative evidence before this court, no evidence whatsoever which could convincingly persuade the Trial Chamber to come to a different conclusion. "The dilemma for the Pusic Defence is that the Trial Chamber must therefore assess Pusic's criminal liability for the crimes he is charged with on the basis of the very same evidence they have already previously found sufficient beyond reasonable doubt." Your Honours, I've read that extract on a number of occasions, and I have to admit to you that I struggle to understand the logic behind the assertion that's made. It's an assertion that's based on the following extract from the Chamber's 98 bis ruling, which states that: "Under Rule 98 bis, the Chamber needs only to determine whether there is evidence on the basis of which any reasonable trier of fact could enter a conviction beyond reasonable doubt. The Trial Chamber believes that at this stage, the Trial Chamber is not to establish whether it would enter a conviction at the end of the trial, but whether it could do so." Your Honours, I don't intend to lecture you on the Tribunal's jurisprudence relating to Rule 98 bis. We do have some slides prepared. I can summarise the position the Chamber took. The Chamber emphasised that it was not part of their duty to consider the probative value of the evidence in the course of determining whether the 98 bis test had been met. The second point that was emphasised in your decision, Your Honours, was that the Chamber only needs to find that there is evidence supporting conviction on the basis of one mode of responsibility. The final point in respect of this particular submission is that, Your Honours, in the course of your decision, it was also emphasised that there is no contradiction between a decision to dismiss a 98 bis motion and a judgement of acquittal, and reference is made to the decision of the Appeals Chamber in Jelic - I'm grateful to Mr. Mulalic - Jelic in that particular case. In summary, Your Honours, we say that the decision that you took in respect of our application under Rule 98 bis should have no bearing on your deliberations at this particular stage of this trial. Before we move on to embark on an analysis of the evidence in this case insofar as it relates to Mr. Pusic, I would also like to make a number of preliminary points, the first of which is to clarify the general nature of our defence. Your Honours, this is not a case where we deny that Mr. Pusic signed documents or issued paperwork, and this is not a case where we challenge the authenticity of all the documents the Prosecution seek to rely on. Where we do challenge the authenticity of any documents, we have tried to explain why it is that we object. And, Your Honours, you will have heard how the Prosecution have attacked the other accused for often adopting what they describe as an unrealistic stance by claiming that large volumes of documents were forgeries. Well, we haven't taken that approach, but it does seem, Your Honours, that the Prosecution is determined to attack us nevertheless. Furthermore, when we have questioned a witness's veracity, we have made it clear what parts of a witness's testimony that we say are unreliable. So, for instance, in relation to witnesses Masovic, Josip Praljak, or Cupina, Praljak being a case in point, is discussed at paragraphs 131 to 136 of our final trial brief - we have said that there are certain aspects of those individuals' testimony that we deem to be unreliable, and we have explained why we take that position. And, Your Honours, as professional judges, you will know from your own experience that an intelligent witness may not lie about everything because an intelligent witness will know that a half lie is often more convincing than an outright lie. So in the case of Josip Praljak, while we don't accept the veracity of everything he says, we do make it clear that when he's testifying about any matter that could potentially inculpate him or his colleague, Bozic, then his words should not be relied on. If I can turn now to the issue of documentary evidence. We ask you to look beyond a literal reading of the documents. We ask you to look beyond blind acceptance of the assertions made by the Prosecution. One of the chief distinguishing characteristics of this trial is the huge volume of documentation, and one of the striking characteristics of this particular conflict is the fact that both sides were armed with battalions of photocopiers, legions of secretaries, as well as conventional weapons. The documents that have been produced in their thousands, as a consequence, don't tell the entire story without further reference to the testimony of the witnesses that have been called in the course of this trial. It also follows, in our submission, that where there is no witness testimony to corroborate the contents of a document, that that document -- the contents of that document should not be taken at face value. So, Your Honours, we ask you to try and place the documentary evidence against Mr. Pusic in the framework of the evidence, as a whole, and against the background of the testimony of all the witnesses that have appeared in this trial. Your Honours, at paragraph 347 of our final trial brief, we alert the Chamber to the fact that there are a number of other individuals who feature in this case who share the same surname as Mr. Pusic, and at paragraph 347 we develop that point in more detail. Having considered the contents of the Prosecution's final trial brief, we have noted that on at least two instances, it appears that the Prosecution have confused Mr. Pusic with someone else. At paragraph 21 of the Prosecution's final trial brief, in an extract referring to a document P2293 regarding deportations, and at footnote 37, and also at paragraph 28 of the Prosecution's final trial brief, at footnote 51, Mr. Pusic is confused with another individual called Mile Pusic. Another example of this can be found at paragraph 595 of the Prosecution's final trial brief in connection with footnote 1389. There is a mistaken reference to Mr. Pusic when it would appear that the witness who is referred to therein is referring to another individual called Berislav, Berislav Soldo. Your Honours, these are, we suggest, important errors. They are significant because they indicate how willing the Prosecution are to make assertions without checking the facts. And they also indicate, in our submission, how, in the course of this five-year marathon trial, indicates how the Prosecution have lost sight of Mr. Pusic. They have been concentrating so hard on the other accused that the dot representing Mr. Pusic has disappeared off the radar. There was a clear example of this in October 2007. Five months after Witness BC had testified in this courtroom, the Prosecution were moved to file a motion asking for that witness to be recalled, on the basis that due to an oversight of counsel, an important document had not been put. And, Your Honours, you will find further information concerning that particular instance in the Prosecution's motion to admit Exhibit P09848, dated the 23rd of October, 2007. So, Your Honours, in our submission, this is a case where the Chamber will need to subject every single assertion that the Prosecution make, in both their final brief and in their closing submissions, to a very detailed level of scrutiny. The final point in respect to this preliminary discussion. Your Honours, we suggest that it is facile for the Prosecution to say that any defendant involved in these proceedings must have known what was going on at the time, and this is a point that was made in the course of the 98 submissions by the Prosecution. And you'll find a reference at transcript page 27148 to 9. It's something that we suggest is facile because obviously in a large-scale case, it's this: Where essentially the HZ-HB government and its policies are on trial. Almost everyone in the area would have known what was going on, but that shouldn't lead to an assumption that everyone connected with the HVO must be guilty of war crimes. In essence, the Prosecution seem to be saying that, Where there is smoke, there must be fire. But in addition to smoke, there must also be light. And, Your Honours, it is our hope that our submissions shine some light on the evidence and shine some light on Pusic's role in this case. Your Honours, I'm about to move on to another substantially different part of my submissions and to begin dealing with the evidence against Mr. Pusic, so perhaps this is a convenient time for us to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This will be our last break for the day, and it will last 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We continue with our hearing. Please go ahead, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to move on to consider the evidence relating to Mr. Pusic. We have dealt with the evidence thematically in our brief. However, in response to the arguments raised by the Prosecution in their written arguments and in their oral submissions, we propose to deal with those matters in a chronological format. And, Your Honours, we'd like to begin by examining the evidence concerning the involvement of Mr. Pusic in this so-called JCE prior to the 5th of July, 1993, which is an important date because, as you will be aware, it's the date of his appointment as head of the Service of Exchange. During the course of the Prosecution's oral submissions, it was stated that the Pusic Defence's submissions that the lack of any evidence, the paucity of evidence concerning Mr. Pusic's contact with other senior members of the so-called JCE, and the paucity of evidence suggesting that he had any role in the genesis of the purported JCE between 1991 and 1993, it was said by the Prosecution that those submissions were irrelevant and amounted to an irrelevant red herring. The words used by the Prosecution were that: "The argument of not being in the JCE because he was unknown to some witnesses and an accused, it's an irrelevant red herring." We say that that statement is unsustainable. You are entitled, Your Honours, to take into account the absence of any evidence of association with other alleged JCE members. That is something that you may consider to be relevant when you decide if Mr. Pusic was a member of the JCE. And, Your Honours, we say the fact that Mr. Pusic had no contact with Franjo Tudjman, the fact that Slobodan Praljak had never heard of him at the time the indictments were announced, and was indeed very surprised when he first heard that he had also been charged, that is all relevant given the way the Prosecution put this case, because it could potentially rebut any inference that Pusic was a leader or member of the joint criminal enterprise. And, Your Honours, that is an area of our submissions that is described in more detail in our brief -- in our final trial brief submissions at paragraphs 25 to 26 and paragraphs 15 to 16.
