Moving on to take matters chronologically: One of the earliest references to Mr. Pusic is in a SIS report from late 1992, and that's document P0663, dated the 28th of October, 1993. Your Honours, you may recall that that was a report of alleged misconduct involving Mr. Pusic. We query if the contents of that document are relevant to the charges in this particular indictment, given that the report refers to Pusic's alleged activities with the Serbs, and note also, Your Honours, you may recall that the Prosecution have also clarified, in the course of their closing submissions, that Mr. Pusic didn't join the JCE until April 1993, yet they're relying on documentation that dates back to a point far earlier in time in October of 1992. Your Honours, we are going to devote some time to this particular document simply because it's highlighted by the Prosecution in their closing brief at paragraphs 1026, 1193, 1247, and 1267. Our position is that the assertions made by the Prosecution on the basis of this document are not reliable. Firstly, this document is a SIS report which is compiled on the basis of sources that are unknown. And, Your Honours, I don't intend to belabour this point. We have the same position that we adopted in the joint Defence motion that was filed on the 7th of January, 2008, in response to the documentary evidence motion filed by the Prosecution. The second point that we would make in respect to this particular exhibit is that this is a document that the Prosecution should have tendered through a witness. We submit the Prosecution should have brought a witness to testify about these allegations, given that they now form a central plank of their case against Mr. Pusic. May I also clarify, Your Honours, that we do not accept any of the allegations made in this document. We say that no weight whatsoever should be attached to them. However, we will, in the course of my submissions, highlight various contradictions that arise from the Prosecution's reliance on this type of material. One of the characteristics of the Prosecution's presentation of their case, we submit, is that as with this particular document, P0663, there are a number of other critical documents that were never put to witnesses in this case, yet they are now given some prominence in the course of the final arguments, either written or oral. It's a particular cause for concern for the Pusic Defence, given the relatively small amount of time that's been spent focusing on Mr. Pusic, and, Your Honour, it's a cause for concern that the Prosecution place so much emphasis on this type of material when it should have been, could have been, shown to a relevant witness. And, Your Honours, the fact that it wasn't shown to a relevant witness reinforces our submissions to the effect that the Prosecution have failed to meet their evidential burden, that they have taken their eye off the ball when it comes to Mr. Pusic. This is nothing more, this document, than uncorroborated documentary hearsay. And we do note that the Chamber has acknowledged in this decision, in other decisions, to admit documentary evidence, that the Chamber will determine how much weight to attach to this type of material in its final deliberations. At this juncture, Your Honours, we would respectfully ask the Chamber to reflect on the approach taken by the Trial Chamber in the case of Haradinaj. And, Your Honours, you have on the screens in front of you an extract from that trial judgement at paragraph 18. I don't intend to recite the entire contents of that particular extract, save to highlight the last sentence: "As a general rule, the less the Trial Chamber knew about a document, the circumstances of its creation and usage, the less weight it gave to it." And, Your Honours, if I may also refer to the following paragraph -- the next paragraph in that particular decision from the same Trial Chamber, paragraph 19. Once again, I don't intend to read out the entire extract, but, Your Honours, we would refer you to the approach taken by the Haradinaj Trial Chamber, where it was held that: "In general, the Trial Chamber clarified that it attached little, if any, weight to unexplained opinions and untested hearsay, and that an accumulation of such evidence did not necessarily make it stronger." The last point I wish to make about this particular document, P0663, is or relates to what you may consider, Your Honours, to be a lack of consistency in the Prosecution's approach to the weight to be attached to SIS documents in general. We submit that when the Prosecution have adduced a SIS document, when the contents of that document tends to support their case, then it has followed that the Prosecution say that that document is a reliable piece of evidence. However, when, in similar circumstances, the Defence have tried to rely on a SIS document, and I can identify one particular instance when Mr. Karnavas presented a SIS document to try and impeach the Witness Smajkic, and that's -- you will find a reference to that in transcript at page 2882, there was an objection raised by the Prosecution on the basis that that document may have been manufactured and was not, therefore, prima facie reliable. Your Honour, we say that this approach smacks of double standards. Your Honours, we have no doubt that you are faced with a formidable task in going through a mountain of material in the coming months, and that you will go through this material and look at it with great scrutiny, but we hope that you will not fall victim to the Prosecution's suggestions that you find Mr. Pusic guilty based on the assumption, conjecture, or speculation contained in uncorroborated documents such as these. Moreover, whatever the scenario, Your Honours, I submit to you that this amounts to nothing more than a form of gossip, and gossip is too unreliable to use as a basis to convict. Your Honours, if I can pick up now the evidence in April 1993, which is a very important date, according to the Prosecution theory of the case, because it is the date when Mr. Pusic is said to enter the JCE. It's also claimed in the Prosecution's brief that in April 1993, Mr. Pusic held a commanding position with substantial authority in the Military Police Crime Prevention Department and that he was involved in processing detainees and dealing with prisoners. And, Your Honours, you will find a reference to that at paragraph 1194 of the Prosecution's final trial brief. We do not dispute that the evidence shows that Mr. Pusic was employed by the Military Police Crime Prevention Department at that time. However, we do submit that the Prosecution have failed to show what position he held. And we also would like to highlight the fact that the documents that the Prosecution rely on to substantiate their assertion that Mr. Pusic held a commanding position all pre-date -- or generally pre-date April 1993, and I will comment on three of these documents very briefly. The first is P1605. This is a document that we submit confirms little more than the fact that Mr. Pusic was on the payroll of the military police in March 1993. It doesn't tell you what post he occupied. Furthermore, P1393 is a Crime Prevention Department report. It's dated February 1993, and it merely shows that Mr. Pusic was one of three military police personnel interviewing detainees held at the Ljubuski detention facility. The third document is dated the 14th of October, 1992. Your Honours, we will provide you with the reference to that document in due course. We submit that this document does not establish, as the Prosecution allege -- does not establish that Pusic had any powers to order inmates to undertake forced labour assignments. The document refers not to prisoners of war or to detainees in the course of the conflict, but to convicts that were held by the HVO. And, Your Honours, we also would like to put forward this proposition: that there are two recurring patterns in the Prosecution's submissions that these documents highlight. The first is that, again, these three documents are now said to be very important, they are now said to be central to the case against Mr. Pusic, yet they have never been shown to a witness. The second pattern that these documents reveal is that they provide further evidence of the Prosecution making assertions which do not stand up to any close scrutiny. So, Your Honours, in respect to the evidence concerning Mr. Pusic's role with the military police in April 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please slow down, because the French booth is lagging behind you. So please slow down as much as possible, and now please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: I'll just recap, then, Your Honours, on the last point that I was making, which is that: We say that the evidence, at its highest, insofar as it concerns Mr. Pusic's role and function in April 1993, goes to show that Mr. Pusic was employed by the military police as a control officer of unspecified rank and responsibility; nothing more than that. Your Honours, in May 1993, the Prosecution alleged that Mr. Pusic acquired another hat, that he became a permanent liaison officer to UNPROFOR, and this is based on an order that is purportedly issued by Bruno Stojic on the 11th of May, 1993. You'll find further particulars of that allegation at paragraph 13 of the indictment. We submit that this assertion is patently incorrect and it has been flatly contradicted by the evidence of one of the Prosecution's own witnesses from SpaBat. That's Witness BJ. Witness BJ testified that what has been described as an order from Bruno Stojic did not appoint Mr. Pusic to be a permanent liaison officer. It simply put him in charge of contact with UNPROFOR in one particular instance. And, Your Honours, you can find further elaboration/discussion of that point at paragraph 80 of the Pusic Defence final trial brief, and we submit this is yet another instance where the Chamber simply can't rely on the assertions made by the Prosecution. And, Your Honours, despite the fact that this was highlighted in our written final trial brief, this is not an assertion that's been retracted by the Prosecution in their closing oral submissions. This allegation is also a matter of concern because we submit, Your Honours, that it provides an example of the Prosecution expanding their case against Mr. Pusic because it's also claimed in the Prosecution's final trial brief, at paragraph 1204, that Mr. Pusic's role as a liaison officer was wider than that. His dealings were restricted not just to SpaBat. Your Honours, that's an allegation that's not previously -- that has not been previously advanced in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief or in the course of their Rule 98 bis submissions. So this allegation of a wider liaison role is not mentioned at all in the indictment. Your Honours, we submit it's unfair to the accused that he should have to respond to what constitutes, in reality, a fresh allegation, an allegation that should have been particularised at an earlier point. In summary, Your Honours, we submit that the Prosecution should not be allowed to use the indictment as a moving target. The next point in the chronology that we pick up on is the 22nd of April, 1993. That's another key date, as far as the Prosecution is concerned, because they claim that from that point onwards, Mr. Pusic had primary responsibility for exchanges. And you'll find that assertion at paragraph 1196 of the Prosecution's final trial brief. That allegation is based on a document, P02020, which you have before you on the PowerPoint presentation, which states and relays an order from Valentin Coric which states that: "Mr. Pusic is charged with participating on behalf of the Military Police Administration in the exchange of all arrested persons." The critical word there, Your Honours, is "participating." We submit that that's a term that's entirely open to interpretation. And, Your Honours, we raise the question of whether it's reasonable to adduce from this document that Pusic had primary responsibility for exchanges or whether there's another reasonable inference that arises, which is that Pusic was not conferred with any decision-making powers as a consequence of this particular document. Your Honours, we say that the Chamber would need to look at other corroborated evidence, if it exists, to see what the true significance of that order is. Your Honours, in reference to this particular allegation that Mr. Pusic had primary responsibility for exchanges, you'll note that at paragraph 288 of our final trial brief, we highlight the fact that there were a number of other HVO bodies who were also engaged in prisoner exchanges. Most prominently and most importantly -- there were four bodies, but most importantly amongst those four bodies is the HVO Exchange Commission headed by Maric. This is a commission - we have labelled it the Maric Commission - that had been in operation and existence since 1992, and it may be relevant, Your Honours, for you to note that Maric was an individual, who was head of that commission, attended far more sessions of the HZ-HB Cabinet than Mr. Pusic ever did. And, Your Honours, that's a point that's further elaborated on in our brief at paragraph 228. Any examination of Mr. Pusic's role in releases and exchanges, which also form one of the most important limbs of the Prosecution's case, we submit, cannot be -- cannot take place without some consideration of the political context at the time. We take the position that the -- that an examination of the facts reveals that decisions regarding prisoner exchanges and prisoner releases, particularly decisions regarding HVO policy in those areas, those decisions were taken at a far higher level than Mr. Pusic's modest station. And, Your Honours, we would like at this juncture to look at Mr. Pusic's role in an exchange meeting that took place on the 4th of May, 1993, at Jablanica, because careful examination of Mr. Pusic's role in that particular event shows that his input was clearly insignificant. According to the Prosecution, this was a high-level meeting where Mr. Pusic played an important role. And, Your Honours, we've examined this meeting. Our submissions are outlined at paragraph 223 of our final trial brief. You may recall during the course of the Prosecution's final submissions that they played clips from two video-recordings, the first from a video, Exhibit P02187, where it was said that Mr. Pusic could be seen sitting on the same table as other senior members of the BiH Army. However, Your Honours, you may have noticed or you may recall that in the course of that clip, there was no dispute -- there can be no dispute that Pusic was only engaged in a discussion concerning the exchange of the sick and wounded. And this meeting is also important in respect of Pusic's Defence because it does appear to be the first occasion when Mr. Pusic comes across General Petkovic. General Petkovic gave evidence in regards to this meeting, and, Your Honours, you'll see from the PowerPoint presentation screen in front of you that he made it clear, in the course of his evidence, that the first time he came into direct contact with Mr. Pusic was during the course of these talks. General Petkovic also made it clear that his job was such that he didn't have any further contact with Mr. Pusic. And His Honour the Presiding Judge, Judge Antonetti, went on to say: "Very well. Then there's no point in my asking you whether he referred to Greater Croatia, et cetera, talking to you, because you said you hardly ever saw him, so the question doesn't arise." Your Honour, that extract from the trial record can be found at page 49799. Petkovic also gave further evidence about this meeting when he confirmed that Mr. Pusic's role was wholly insignificant, as Pusic's role was restricted to dealing with the sick and injured from Sovici and Doljani. And, Your Honours, you'll find the reference to that would be transcript record page 49501. Your Honours, we submit that General Petkovic had no reason to lie and no reason to minimise Mr. Pusic's role at that particular meeting. The Prosecution say that this was a high-level meeting, but, on the contrary, General Petkovic makes it clear that Mr. Pusic's presence was not considered significant by him. The Chamber may also recall that the same footage from that particular video also contains footage of a dispute between a representative of the HVO, Bagaric, and General Halilovic. There was a heated discussion, and it's clear from that that Mr. Pusic does not feature prominently in that exchange. And, Your Honours, if you -- if you were to examine the Exhibit P02187, between -- from 3:31 to 4:20 or transcript pages 1 to 32 relating to the same exhibit, you would find that there is very little, if no reference to Mr. Pusic in the contents of that particular document. The second video that the Prosecution relied in the course of their submissions concerning the 4th of May meeting in Jablanica was Exhibit P0999. In the course of that video, you may recall that the Prosecution highlighted a reference to Mr. Pusic from a television journalist, where Mr. Pusic was described as a negotiator. Now, Your Honours, we don't necessarily agree that Mr. Pusic was a HVO representative or negotiator, but even if it was -- even if he was, it does not follow that he necessarily had decision-making powers. Your Honours, it's up to the Trial Chamber to decide what the truth is beyond reasonable doubt, but we would ask you to take heed of the careful forensic approach taken by the Milutinovic Trial Chamber when determining the significance and weight to be attached to evidence concerning Milutinovic's participation in numerous meetings. I'm not saying that there were any obvious parallels that can be drawn between the case against Mr. Milutinovic and that against Mr. Pusic. I would only merely suggest that the forensic approach taken by the Milutinovic Trial Chamber should be adopted in this case. At paragraph 25 of the Milutinovic trial judgement, the Trial Chamber noted that Mr. Milutinovic had given two morale-boosting speeches at meetings that he'd attended. However, in the Trial Chamber's view, his conduct did not constitute a significant contribution to the joint criminal enterprise. Nor did the Milutinovic Trial Chamber take the view that Milutinovic's conduct at other meetings had a substantial effect on the commission of other crimes. And, Your Honours, if I can refer you to paragraph 281 of the Milutinovic trial judgement, there is further reference to Milutinovic's conduct in providing a number of morale-boosting speeches to officials, and the trial judgement reads that: "These two factors on their own, however, in the context of such a large case with a multiplicity of players, cannot be said to have had a substantial effect on the commission of the crimes of displacement which were committed from late March 1999 onwards." I would like to turn now to discuss the evidence concerning the events in Mostar that took place between the 7th and 9th of May, 1993. The evidence indicates that Mr. Pusic was still employed by the military police at this time. If we accept the testimony of Josip Praljak, Mr. Pusic's role in the arrest and detention of Muslim residents in Mostar, and their delivery to the Heliodrom, was restricted to their release or to the release of some of the detainees interned between those dates and thereafter in the course of May. Josip Praljak testified that Pusic would regularly telephone him with lists of detainees to be released. The Prosecution seek to draw the inference from that testimony that Pusic had the power to decide who could be released. We question whether that is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from Josip Praljak's evidence, given that Praljak had no knowledge of the internal procedures that Pusic had to follow. And we submit that even if this evidence is taken at its highest, even if Praljak is accepted as credible on this issue, all the evidence shows is that Pusic transmitted lists, lists containing names of detainees to be released, from the military police to Mr. Praljak. And, in any event, even if you were to find that Mr. Pusic was involved in expediting the release of these detainees, we submit that Mr. Pusic acted entirely correctly in doing so. And if I may refer the Chamber to Josip Praljak's testimony on this point in relation to a document P02260. This is a note prepared by Stanko Bozic, recording a call from Pusic, with a request for the release of detainees held at the Heliodrom. In responses to questions from His Honour Judge Antonetti, Josip Praljak confirms that the people that had been detained at this time at the Heliodrom had no place there and should have been released. To be more precise, he's asked: "What I'm saying is, if Mr. Pusic acted as is written down in the Official Note, was that the right decision when he said --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, what is the problem? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could everyone please say "Josip Praljak," because later on a confusion might arise, because there's Slobodan Praljak and there's Josip Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: I apologise to General Praljak. I'll try and take heed of his observation. Josip Praljak testified, in response to the question from His Honour Judge Antonetti, that: "Well, not only those people, but none of the other people either should have been there." He was then asked: "And then you testified that the people left Heliodrom very quickly after that, these people?" He answered: "Yes." Your Honours, the evidence shows that almost all those civilians that were detained between the 7th to the 9th of May, 1993, were released by the end of that month. Subsequent to that, subsequent to the events of the 7th to the 9th of May, there were meetings, a number of negotiations between HVO and BiH representatives that continued until the end of June. In our final brief, we have examined the evidence concerning Mr. Pusic's role at these meetings, and we submit that although Mr. Pusic may have been present at some of these exchange meetings, the facts of his involvement do not support the Prosecution's case that he had primary responsibility for prisoner exchanges. Indeed, the evidence indicates that at the high-level meetings that took place after the 12th of May, 1993, meetings that were to arrange the release of those Muslims arrested in Mostar and other issues such as humanitarian aid, the evidence suggests that General Petkovic and Halilovic were the main negotiators until Delic replaced Halilovic in June 1993. Your Honours, we also submit that there is a valid distinction to be made between high-level negotiations that were taking place at this time and low-level talks that were also occurring, and the distinction is one that is identified by the Prosecution Witness Watkins and also by Prosecution Witness Masovic. Our case is that Mr. Pusic was involved primarily in low-level talks, where he dealt with lower-ranking BiH officials such as Alikadic. And, Your Honours, we have developed those submissions in more detail at paragraphs 56 to 58 of our final trial brief and also at paragraphs 74 to 81. But there is one point that highlights our submissions, and this is the fact that there is no evidence that Mr. Pusic attended any of the highest-level talks in Geneva throughout 1993 or any of the highest-level talks in Sarajevo, talks that normally took place at Sarajevo Airport. Your Honours, any discussion of exchange negotiations in 1993 must also include some reference to political machinations occurring at the various highest diplomatic and political levels. We submit that there is very little evidence to link Mr. Pusic to key events and meetings at those levels throughout the entire indictment period. There is, for instance, no link between Mr. Pusic and the talks that took place on the 20th of July, 1993, between Galbraith and Boban, and on the same date, Izetbegovic issues a decision for the release of all captured soldiers and civilians. And, Your Honours, that's a point that is developed at paragraph 243 of our final trial brief. There's also no link between Mr. Pusic and the joint agreement signed by Tudjman and Izetbegovic on the 14th of September, 1993, one of the major milestones in the course of the negotiations between the HVO and the ABiH during the course of that summer. It's also relevant to note, we submit, that on the following day, on the 15th of September, 1993, Mate Boban issues an order to ensure that the conditions at the detention centres run by the HVO are compatible with the requirements of International Humanitarian Law. The order also requires ICRC to have access to all facilities. What is particularly relevant about this order is -- as far as the Pusic Defence is concerned, is the fact that it's not circulated to Berislav Pusic. And again, Your Honours, we would refer you to paragraphs 240 and 243 of our final trial brief. The document in question is P5104. One of the Prosecution's main witnesses in relation to Mr. Pusic's role concerning prisoner release and exchanges is Cupina. Cupina claimed that Pusic was the Alpha and Omega of release and exchange matters, and that's a quote, Your Honours, that's cited in the Prosecution's final trial brief at paragraph 1209, and it's a quote that was repeated in the course of -- it's repeated in the course of their closing submissions, and that's transcript reference 44908. Cupina's evidence is dealt with in our trial brief at paragraphs 188 to 197, and we've dealt with his evidence in some detail. In summary, we say that his testimony is incapable of belief. And we note that the Chamber has already recognised that they have reservations about his credibility that may seriously affect the reliability of his testimony, and we rely on a decision rendered by the Trial Chamber on the 3rd of November, 2006, in response to a request from the Defence for General Praljak. Your Honours, we suggest that no weight should be given to the evidence of Mr. Cupina. Your Honour, in relation to events before the 5th of July, the last document that I want to refer to briefly is P02546. This was referred to in the course of the Prosecution's closing oral submissions, and that reference can be found at transcript page 52148. The document is a report on the activities of the HVO military police, dated the 28th of May, 1993. It records that an order had been received from Berislav Pusic and Coric to transfer the prisoners to the prisons on the Heliodrom. In their interpretation of this document in their closing submissions, the Prosecution put Mr. Coric and Mr. Pusic on the same footing, and, Your Honours, we highlight that because we suggest and submit it's important for the Trial Chamber to know that there are contradictions in both the Prosecution's final brief and in their closing arguments in regard to what they claim the positions are taken by each of the co-accused, and we raise the question of whether the only inference that can be drawn from this document is the inference that Mr. Pusic had decision-making authority, or whether there is any other reasonable inference available from this material; namely, that Mr. Pusic's role was restricted to that of a messenger in this scenario. I would now like to move on to the second phase of our submissions, which deals with the evidence concerning events after the 5th of July, 1993, which is the date that Mr. Pusic is appointed head of the Service of Exchange. Your Honours, if I could briefly make a general observation about the Service of Exchange and also the 6th of August, 1993, commission. Our position is that Mr. Pusic had no de jure or de facto powers arising as a consequence of either appointment. The titles that he was given may sound grand, but we would remind you of a quote from George McGovern, the American politician, who said that: "The longer the job title, the less important the job." Your Honour, the Service for Exchange was conceived on the 5th of July, 1993, and we submit that from that very moment onwards, there is no evidence that Mr. Pusic was conferred with any de jure authority over any limb of the HVO military apparatus, that he had no de jure authority over any military personnel as a consequence of that appointment, and, Your Honours, we also submit that the evidence suggests that the Service for Exchange was not part of the civilian structure either. The evidence does not show that the Service for Exchange was required to report to the HVO HZ-HB Cabinet, and that's a point that we have outlined at paragraph 85 of our closing submissions. The evidence does not show that, as a consequence of his appointment to the Service for Exchange, Mr. Pusic was subordinated and required to report to Jadranko Prlic. The evidence suggests that the Service for Exchange was a stand-alone body, and we say that that conclusion is entirely consistent with its role as a service providing technical advice. It was the Prosecution's expert, Tomljanovich, who confirmed that the Service for Exchange's remit was strictly defined at the time it was created, and it was strictly defined, in his words, so that the service was: "... charged with providing the technical support for the HVO HZ-HB, in particular the Commission for Exchange of Prisoners and Other Persons ." Your Honours, it's up to you to decide if you consider our use of a selective quote from the Prosecution's own expert to be unfair. Turning now to the 6th of August, 1993, commission, this is another important moment in the Prosecution's case. The Prosecution allege that as a consequence of this appointment, Mr. Pusic began releasing detainees. And, Your Honours, you'll find a reference to that at paragraph 595 of the Prosecution's final trial brief. The Prosecution also contend that Mr. Pusic's appointment amounts to a natural expansion of his role. Further elaboration of that can be found at paragraph 1202 of the Prosecution's final trial brief. During their oral closing submissions, the Prosecution said as follows: "Bruno Stojic, he placed the responsibility and power to release and exchange prisoners upon Mr. Pusic's shoulders when he set up the commission on the 6th of August, 1993. And that's Exhibit P03995. Mr. Pusic exercised this responsibility throughout the rest of 1993. He often did this without following the outlined procedures, as we have seen, of engaging with the SIS and military police concurrence or involving other commission members." Your Honours, that's transcript reference 52156. Your Honours, we submit that the evidence of Josip Praljak points to the fact that the commission never took effect and existed only on paper. Josip Praljak gave evidence about his role in the commission, because he was appointed as one of its five members, and said as follows. He was asked: "But let me go back. When you received this order," this is an order notifying him of his appointment to the commission, "you said that you talked to Mr. Pusic over the telephone about the work of that commission and that Mr. Pusic said, 'We'll do the work.'" He answered: "Yes." "After that, had you no further contact with Mr. Pusic in respect to this commission, did you, nor do you mention this in your diary at all? I find no entry to that effect." He answered: "No, we never had a meeting." And that's transcript reference 14974. Josip Praljak went on to say that he had no further contact with Mr. Pusic regarding the work of the commission and that Mr. Pusic never wrote to him concerning the commission. Praljak continued and confirmed that he never spoke to or met with any other members of the commission in an official capacity. And, Your Honours, that's a point that we've explored in further detail at paragraph 96 of our final trial brief. Other factors that the Trial Chamber may wish to take into account when considering what weight to attach to this evidence concerning the commission relates to the absence of any documentation produced by it and to the fact that the commission is never referred to in any HVO HZ-HB Cabinet meetings. And, Your Honours, that is a point that we have outlined at paragraphs 100 to 103 of our final trial brief. It's also interesting to note that the Prosecution's position on the 6th of August commission seems to be somewhat contradictory. At paragraph 319 of the final trial brief, the Prosecution assert that: "In fact, Pusic's commission never convened, a fact commission member made known to Stojic." Your Honours, it's not clear, in light of that reference, whether the Prosecution agree with the submissions advanced by the Defence, that the commission never functioned at all, or whether they don't. It's also correct to say that the Prosecution never challenged the evidence of Josip Praljak on this point. We submit the Prosecution can't have it both ways and that this evidence goes to show, once again, that the Prosecution have failed to discharge their evidential burden, that they have taken their eye off their ball when they're dealing with Mr. Pusic. On the 12th of August, 1993, the Prosecution allege that Mr. Pusic prepared a proposal concerning the work of the commission, and this document is Exhibit P04141, and it's a document that's referred to in the indictment at paragraph 17.6(G). Your Honours, we don't intend to dwell on this particular document, because we say that far too much significance has been given to it by the Prosecution. It is just a proposal. There is no evidence that proposal was ever acted on. This document does not, in our submission, establish that Pusic had any decision-making powers. And, Your Honours, a review of the evidence concerning, for instance, the categorising and cataloging of prisoners suggests that there were other HVO bodies that were actually responsible for those tasks. Concerning prisoner exchanges in the latter half of 1993, there are two inter-connected limbs of the Prosecution's case that we would like to address. At paragraph 1249 of the Prosecution's final trial brief, it said that Mr. Pusic obstructed and frustrated exchanges, and one of the ways he is alleged to have achieved this is through advocating -- insisting on "one for one" exchanges. We will deal with the wider allegation of obstruction first. And, Your Honours, may I ask that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Our submissions in respect of "one for one" exchanges are outlined in detail in our final trial brief at paragraphs 62 to 70. In short, we say that the evidence demonstrates that both sides had fluid negotiating positions when it came to discussing the terms of prisoner exchanges. And this is a submission that we haven't ventilated in our final trial brief, but our argument, Your Honours, is that both sides in these negotiations contributed to their failure, and thus it is, therefore, unfair to attribute responsibility to Mr. Pusic, particularly in light of evidence that suggests that he had no unilateral powers, that he was simply passing on instructions from above. Your Honours, in this respect we refer you to the approach taken by the Milutinovic Trial Chamber when considering Milutinovic's responsibility for the collapse of negotiations. Again, I'm not drawing any parallels between the two cases, but respectfully drawing your attention to an approach that was taken when examining evidence by another Trial Chamber. The judgement states: "Addressing his contribution first, the Chamber is of the view that a number of examples of Milutinovic's participation in the joint criminal enterprise alleged by the Prosecution have not been proved beyond reasonable doubt. For example, the Chamber found that, during the negotiations between Kosovo Albanians and the FRY/Serbian authorities, all sides contributed to their failure. As a result, the Chamber was unable to find that Milutinovic obstructed the negotiating process." And that's paragraph 274. The Prosecution try and link Mr. Pusic's role in prisoner exchanges and releases with their claim that at the heart of the JCE lay the desire to ethnically cleanse parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And, Your Honours, they make this allegation a number of different ways, using very imaginative and fluid language. In paragraph 1231 of the Prosecution's final trial brief, it said that Mr. Pusic is a demographic engineer who had the power to give permission for people to depart. At paragraph 1243 of the final trial brief, it said that Mr. Pusic launched a deportation scheme with Valentin Coric. And there are a number of other variations on this theme, as if reformulation and repetition will improve the Prosecution's case. Our position is that while Mr. Pusic may have had some involvement in issuing discharge letters for some, but not all, detainees in this time-frame in the latter half of 1993, the evidence does not show that Mr. Pusic had any say in determining where those detainees went after they left custody. In particular, we submit that the Prosecution has failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that Mr. Pusic had any involvement in issuing letters of guarantees or transit visas for those leaving HVO detention. In our final trial brief at paragraphs 151 to 154, we have examined the evidence as to who was actually responsible for issuing transit visas and letters of guarantee, and I do not intend to rehash those submissions here. I will, however, refer the Chamber to the evidence of Josip Praljak which we submit shows that Mr. Pusic's role was strictly limited to checking whether a detainee had the approval of SIS and the CPD before he could issue a discharge letter. At transcript reference 14713, and unfortunately we don't have a slide for this quote, Josip Praljak was asked: "What approvals were required, to your knowledge, to have a prisoner release from the Heliodrom in July/August 1993? You can just walk us through whatever steps were taken, if you can help us, please." "The document that would reach us in the prison was formulated like this, approximately. There is no reason to hold the prisoner of war such and such, and it would be signed by Miroslav Music on behalf of the SIS and Vidovic on behalf of the Crime Investigation Service. They would issue approvals enabling Mr. Pusic to release somebody. I believe without these two signatures above, Mr. Pusic would have been unable to release anyone." Your Honours, that's a transcript reference that can be found at paragraph 303 of our final trial brief. You may also recall, Your Honours, that you heard from another witness, Vidovic, who confirmed that the Crime Prevention Department had to issue a certificate certifying that they had no objection to the release of a detainee. And, Your Honours, that reference can be found at transcript pages 51690. Your Honours, in the course of their closing submissions, the Prosecution referred to a number of documents emanating from the SIS service that they claim prove that Mr. Pusic had the power to order releases unilaterally without obtaining consent from SIS and the CID. I'd like to consider one of these documents. The first document is P6170. This is a document that doesn't emanate from SIS. It's a report from Josip Praljak, where he acknowledged that he was mistaken in his evidence concerning Pusic's role in the release of a number of detainees. Your Honours, Josip Praljak's evidence can be found at transcript reference 14980, and our submissions are outlined in our final trial brief at paragraph 312. The second document the Prosecution referred to, again, is not a SIS document. It's a newspaper article dated the 19th of October, 1993, and that's Exhibit reference P5945. In the course of this article, Pusic is said to contrast his powers to make decisions on prisoner exchanges with that of his BiH counterparts, who had no such powers. Your Honours, you may find it interesting to contrast, yourselves, what Pusic says about the extent of his own influence in that interview, P5945, with what another witness says. If I may ask, Your Honours, for the Chamber to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank Madam Registrar. We will continue with Mr. Pusic's closing arguments tomorrow morning. We begin at 9.00. Until then, I wish you all a nice evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of February, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 25
